title: A letter unread (Berakhot 55a–b)
hookLine: a dream not interpreted is like a letter not read; dreams follow their reading
tomorrow: what three things bring a worn-out person back to themselves?

cards: The red badge on the mail app says forty-one unread. Some of those are nothing. One of them might matter.
Now a dream you never think about again: is it a letter unopened? Rav Chisda says yes, almost word for word. A dream that isn't interpreted is like a letter that isn't read.
And the very same pages hold the other side of the argument.

teach.b: Here are both views, each at its best. First, the letter. Rav Chisda's point is that a dream is addressed to you, and leaving it sealed wastes it.
The Talmud pushes further: dreams follow their reading. It tells of a sage, Rabbi Bana'ah, who had a dream and took it to the dream interpreters in Jerusalem.
The Talmud says there were twenty-four of them. Each read it differently, and every reading came true. So the reading isn't just decoding.
It shapes. That's the case for opening the letter, and opening it kindly. Now the other side, also on these pages.
Just as there's no grain without straw, there's no dream without some nonsense in it.

teach.h: THE THOUGHTS OF YOUR OWN HEART.
teach.b: And another sage says a person is shown in a dream only what comes from the thoughts of their own heart. On that view, the dream is mostly your own mind talking at night: worth hearing, not worth obeying.
Here's what's striking. The Talmud doesn't make these two fight to the death.
A letter can still be mostly straw, and a dream from your own heart can still tell you what's in it. Read it, and read it kindly, because the reading leads.

how: The Talmud's chapter on dreams sits in Berakhot; some Jews, after an upsetting dream, say a traditional prayer during the priestly blessing in synagogue, or have a dream 'made good' (hatavat chalom) before three friends.

o: a prayer someone forgot to finish before falling asleep
a love letter that was written but never sent
a dream no one interprets, left unopened like mail

games.q: two views of a dream — tap the pairs.
p: a dream not read is a letter not read
many readings, every one came true

s: the Talmud says every dream is a message from God
it also says no dream is without straw, and dreams show the thoughts of your own heart.
the Talmud says dreams follow their reading
Rabbi Bana'ah's one dream got many readings, and every one came true.
the Talmud says dreams are just nonsense, so ignore them
Rav Chisda calls an uninterpreted dream a letter left unread.

games.q: your little brother dreams he fails his driving test, which is tomorrow. he wants to cancel. one cousin says it's a sign; another says dreams are random noise. what do these pages hold?
o: cancel: Rav Chisda teaches that a dream is a message that will happen.
ignore it completely: the Talmud says dreams are only straw.
both: it's his own worry talking, so read it kindly, as nerves, and go.
games.why: Berakhot holds both: a dream is a letter worth reading, and it shows the thoughts of your own heart, with straw mixed in. and dreams follow their reading, so give it a kind one.

practice: Bring back one dream, even a scrap of one. With a pen, write a single sentence that reads it kindly, as a letter from your own heart about what you care about. Then sit with that sentence and leave the straw where it fell.

wordCard.voice: A letter unread: Rav Chisda's picture of a dream no one interprets, and the reminder that dreams follow their reading.

orig.note: Hebrew: dream; 'a dream not interpreted is like a letter not read.'

carryVoice: Tuck this away: a letter unread is still addressed to you, so read it kindly. Thirty-five.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 55a (Rav Chisda: a dream not interpreted is like a letter not read; no grain without straw)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 55b (Rabbi Bana'ah and the twenty-four dream interpreters of Jerusalem; dreams follow the mouth; a person is shown only the thoughts of his heart)
